verifiedClaims.claim: The statute provides that if a dog bites or otherwise attacks a person who is in a public place or is lawfully on private property (including the property of the dog's owner), the owner is liable for the resulting damages regardless of the animal's prior behavior or the owner's knowledge of any tendency toward aggression.
verifiedClaims.note: S.C. Code § 47-3-110(A): 'If a person is bitten or otherwise attacked by a dog while the person is in a public place or is lawfully in a private place, including the property of the dog owner or person having the dog in the person's care or keeping, the dog owner or person having the dog in the person's care or keeping is liable for the damages suffered by the person bitten or otherwise attacked.' (B): the section does not apply if 'the person who was attacked provoked or harassed the dog and that provocation was the proximate cause of the attack' or to a qualifying law-enforcement dog. (1986 Act No. 343; amended 2013 Act No. 62.) The statute has no knowledge element, so 'regardless of prior behavior' is its effect. Optional precision: liability also runs to the 'person having the dog in the person's care or keeping', and 'lawfully' covers a person there on a legal duty (e.g., a mail carrier) or by express or implied invitation of the owner, tenant or resident.

verifiedClaims.claim: The defendant owned or had custody of the dog.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 47-3-110(A); Harris v. Anderson County Sheriff's Office, 381 S.C. 357 (2009), as quoted in Clea v. Odom (2011)
verifiedClaims.note: Statute: 'dog owner or person having the dog in the person's care or keeping'. Harris: 'care or keeping' requires that the other person 'act in a manner which manifests an acceptance of responsibility for the care or keeping of the dog'. 'Custody' is a fair gloss.

verifiedClaims.claim: The victim did not provoke the dog.

verifiedClaims.note: The list is introduced by 'The only elements the victim must establish are:'. Either move provocation out of the list ('The owner can avoid liability only by showing the victim provoked or harassed the dog and that this caused the attack') or reword the bullet to 'The victim did not provoke or harass the dog into the attack.' Low word growth.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina courts have recognized that a landlord may be liable for a tenant's dog attack when the landlord knew or had reason to know that a dangerous dog was on the property and had the ability to remove the animal or require the tenant to do so.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina's general rule is the opposite: 'a landlord is not liable to a tenant's invitee for injuries inflicted by an animal kept by a tenant on leased property' (Clea v. Odom, 394 S.C. 175, 714 S.E.2d 542 (2011), citing Gilbert v. Miller (Ct. App. 2003) and Bruce v. Durney (Ct. App. 2000)). Knowing the dog is vicious and being able to end the tenancy is not enough: Mitchell v. Bazzle, 304 S.C. 402, 404 S.E.2d 910 (Ct. App. 1991), reversed a verdict against a landlord who knew of the dog's vicious propensities and could have terminated the month-to-month lease, rejecting that (California, Uccello) theory; Fair v. United States, 334 S.C. 321 (1999), held the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act did not change the rule. Two recognized exceptions (Clea): (1) common-law negligence where the attack happens in a common area the landlord controls and the landlord had actual knowledge of the dog's vicious propensity and failed to remedy it; (2) strict liability under § 47-3-110 where the landlord exercised control over the premises and assumed responsibility for the care or keeping of the dog (Harris v. Anderson County Sheriff's Office, 381 S.C. 357 (2009)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Clea v. Odom, 394 S.C. 175, 714 S.E.2d 542 (2011); Mitchell v. Bazzle, 304 S.C. 402, 404 S.E.2d 910 (Ct. App. 1991), cert. dismissed, 306 S.C. 407 (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: This sentence states the rule Mitchell v. Bazzle rejected. Suggested: 'South Carolina landlords are generally not liable for a tenant's dog. The South Carolina Supreme Court has recognized two exceptions: a landlord who controls a common area where the attack happens and knew the dog was vicious but did nothing, and a landlord who took on the care or keeping of the dog (Clea v. Odom, 2011).' Mitchell: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1348382/mitchell-v-bazzle/

verifiedClaims.claim: The landlord was aware of prior complaints about the dog's aggressive behavior from neighbors or other tenants.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Knowledge is necessary but not sufficient: in Clea the landlord's actual knowledge (the dog had previously attacked a child) mattered because the attack happened in a common area he controlled; in Mitchell v. Bazzle knowledge plus the power to end the lease did not create liability.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Clea v. Odom (2011); Mitchell v. Bazzle (Ct. App. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Keep only as part of the common-area exception: 'The landlord knew the dog had attacked or threatened someone before.'

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault system: a victim can recover damages as long as their share of fault is less than 51 percent.

(1991) adopted modified comparative negligence for negligence actions: a plaintiff recovers if his or her negligence 'is not greater than that of the defendant', reduced in proportion. No South Carolina appellate decision was located applying comparative fault to reduce a § 47-3-110 strict-liability recovery; the statute's own victim-conduct rule is the all-or-nothing provocation exception.

Claims involving minors are typically tolled (paused) until the child reaches the age of majority,
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina: the time a child is under 18 does not count, but the period cannot be extended 'in any case longer than one year after the disability ceases' — so a child's claim must be filed by the later of three years from the bite or the child's 19th birthday (S.C. Code § 15-3-40). Georgia: the two-year period is tolled until the child turns 18 (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90), so the deadline is the 20th birthday.
verifiedClaims.note: 'Paused until the age of majority' implies a fresh full period at 18; in SC it is only one year. Suggested: 'A child's claim in South Carolina generally must be filed by the later of three years from the bite or the child's 19th birthday (S.C. Code § 15-3-40); in Georgia, by age 20.' Georgia does require ante-litem notice: 12 months for the State (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26), 12 months for counties (§ 36-11-1), 6 months for cities (§ 36-33-5). Separately, § 47-3-110(B)(2) exempts a police K-9 bite made in full compliance with a lawful handler command and agency policy, unless the bite is on a third-party bystander.
verifiedClaims.note: The example is odd: a government employee's own pet is a private-owner claim, not a government claim. Use a realistic example (a county animal shelter dog, or a police K-9). Odom, 394 S.C. 175, 714 S.E.2d 542 (2011), citing Gilbert v. Miller (Ct. App. 2003) and Bruce v. Durney (Ct. App. 2000)). Knowing the dog is vicious and being able to end the tenancy is not enough: Mitchell v. Bazzle, 304 S.C. 402, 404 S.E.2d 910 (Ct. App. 1991), reversed a verdict against a landlord who knew of the dog's vicious propensities and could have terminated the month-to-month lease, rejecting that (California, Uccello) theory; Fair v. United States, 334 S.C. 321 (1999), held the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act did not change the rule. Two recognized exceptions (Clea): (1) common-law negligence where the attack happens in a common area the landlord controls and the landlord had actual knowledge of the dog's vicious propensity and failed to remedy it; (2) strict liability under § 47-3-110 where the landlord exercised control over the premises and assumed responsibility for the care or keeping of the dog (Harris v. Odom, 394 S.C. 175, 714 S.E.2d 542 (2011), citing Gilbert v. Miller (Ct. App. 2003) and Bruce v. Durney (Ct. App. 2000)). Knowing the dog is vicious and being able to end the tenancy is not enough: Mitchell v. Bazzle, 304 S.C. 402, 404 S.E.2d 910 (Ct. App. 1991), reversed a verdict against a landlord who knew of the dog's vicious propensities and could have terminated the month-to-month lease, rejecting that (California, Uccello) theory; Fair v. United States, 334 S.C. 321 (1999), held the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act did not change the rule. Two recognized exceptions (Clea): (1) common-law negligence where the attack happens in a common area the landlord controls and the landlord had actual knowledge of the dog's vicious propensity and failed to remedy it; (2) strict liability under § 47-3-110 where the landlord exercised control over the premises and assumed responsibility for the care or keeping of the dog (Harris v. Anderson County Sheriff's Office, 381 S.C. 357 (2009)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Clea v. Odom (2011); Mitchell v. Bazzle (Ct. App. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Knowledge alone is not enough. Suggested: 'Landlords are generally not liable for a tenant's dog, but may be if the attack happened in a common area they control and they knew the dog was dangerous (Clea v. Odom, 2011).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia requires proof of the owner's knowledge of vicious propensity (O.C.G.A. § 51-2-7).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 51-2-7 requires proof the dog was 'vicious or dangerous' and was carelessly managed or allowed to go at liberty; a local leash or at-heel ordinance violation is 'sufficient' proof of vicious propensity without proof of the owner's prior knowledge.
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Georgia requires proof that the dog was dangerous — usually the owner's knowledge of prior aggression, or a leash-law violation (O.C.G.A. § 51-2-7).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Provocation is a defense in both states.
South Carolina's filing deadline is three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530); Georgia allows two years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33).

Yes. Under S.C. Code section 47-3-110, a dog owner is strictly liable for injuries caused by their dog if the victim was in a public place or lawfully on private property. The owner is liable even if the dog has never bitten before.
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Optional: 'and did not provoke the dog'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Medical expenses, plastic surgery and scar revision costs, lost wages, pain and suffering, emotional distress, and in severe cases involving children, long-term psychological treatment costs.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. common law of compensatory damages; no statutory cap on ordinary personal-injury damages against private defendants
verifiedClaims.note: Generic damages list; nothing to verify.

verifiedClaims.claim: Potentially, if the landlord knew the tenant had a dangerous dog and failed to act, or if the lease prohibited dogs and the landlord failed to enforce it.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina's general rule is the opposite: 'a landlord is not liable to a tenant's invitee for injuries inflicted by an animal kept by a tenant on leased property' (Clea v. Odom, 394 S.C. 175, 714 S.E.2d 542 (2011), citing Gilbert v. Miller (Ct. App. 2003) and Bruce v. Durney (Ct. App. 2000)). Knowing the dog is vicious and being able to end the tenancy is not enough: Mitchell v. Bazzle, 304 S.C. 402, 404 S.E.2d 910 (Ct. App. 1991), reversed a verdict against a landlord who knew of the dog's vicious propensities and could have terminated the month-to-month lease, rejecting that (California, Uccello) theory; Fair v. United States, 334 S.C. 321 (1999), held the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act did not change the rule. Two recognized exceptions (Clea): (1) common-law negligence where the attack happens in a common area the landlord controls and the landlord had actual knowledge of the dog's vicious propensity and failed to remedy it; (2) strict liability under § 47-3-110 where the landlord exercised control over the premises and assumed responsibility for the care or keeping of the dog (Harris v. Anderson County Sheriff's Office, 381 S.C. 357 (2009)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Clea v. Odom (2011); Mitchell v. Bazzle (Ct. App. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Both theories are unsupported in SC (Mitchell rejected knowledge + failure to act on the lease; no case on unenforced pet clauses). Suggested: 'Usually not. A South Carolina landlord can be liable only in narrow cases — for example, if the attack happened in a common area the landlord controls and the landlord knew the dog was dangerous and did nothing.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Provocation is a defense. If you provoked the dog, your recovery may be reduced or barred under comparative fault. SC allows recovery if your fault is less than 51 percent.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Under § 47-3-110(B)(1), provocation or harassment that was the proximate cause of the attack bars the statutory claim entirely — it is not a comparative-fault reduction. Comparative fault (Nelson, less than 51%) is a separate rule for negligence claims; its application to the strict-liability claim is unsettled.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 47-3-110(B)(1); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Suggested: 'Provocation is a defense. If you provoked or harassed the dog and that caused the attack, the South Carolina statute does not apply. In a negligence claim, your recovery is reduced by your share of fault and barred at 51 percent or more.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Three years in SC. Two years in Georgia.
verifiedClaims.note: FAQPage structured data. Exceptions (minors, government defendants) are covered in the body.

verifiedClaims.claim: Seek medical attention immediately for wound care and infection prevention. Report the bite to animal control. Document the dog, owner, and location. Photograph your injuries. Get witness information.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 47-5-90; SC DPH — Reporting and Treating Animal Bites
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate. Optional: 'Report the bite to animal control and the S.C. Department of Public Health.' FAQPage structured data.

recommendedEdits: Landlord section (body, Key Takeaways, both landlord FAQs): replace the knowledge-plus-ability-to-remove rule with South Carolina's actual rule — landlords are generally not liable for a tenant's dog (Clea v. Odom, 394 S.C. 175 (2011); Mitchell v. Bazzle, 304 S.C. 402 (Ct. App. 1991)); exceptions are a controlled common area plus actual knowledge, or the landlord taking on care or keeping of the dog (then § 47-3-110 strict liability can apply). Delete the 'pet policy not enforced' and 'renewed the lease' bullets; fix the meta FAQ answer (FAQPage schema).

Provocation: add 'or harassed' and the proximate-cause requirement (§ 47-3-110(B)(1)); move provocation out of the victim's 'elements' list; drop the categorical 'approaching or petting is not provocation' (no SC authority); meta FAQ — provocation bars the statutory claim, it is not a comparative-fault reduction.
Comparative fault: hedge Nelson's 51% rule as applying to negligence claims (no SC case applying it to § 47-3-110); keep the $100,000 → $70,000 example with the hedge.

Deadlines: minors — SC is the later of 3 years or the 19th birthday (§ 15-3-40), GA the 20th birthday (§ 9-3-90); government — SC Tort Claims Act 2-year limit (§ 15-78-110), GA ante-litem notice 6/12 months; replace the 'government employee's dog' example.

Georgia comparison: Key Takeaway should mention the leash-law alternative; replace the Georgia trespasser cell (§ 51-2-7 has no trespasser/tort clause); soften 'sits close to the Georgia border'.
Bite-force line: '200 pounds per square inch' has no source and the wrong unit — drop or cite Lindner 1995 (up to ~313 lbf).

Bite reporting FAQ: name the right agencies — S.C. Department of Public Health (mandatory report within one working day, § 47-5-90) plus Charleston Police Department or Charleston County Sheriff's Office animal control.
